question_text:
Historians of Corrastane Roads have long explained the harbor master's custom of tolling the mole bell during fog as a navigation aid, a warning to captains standing off the Gannet Shoals. Yet the neighboring harbor of Merholt, bounded by the same shoals and wrapped in fog as often, never kept a bell, and its captains ran aground no more frequently. The harbor master's day-book also shows that the bell was tolled only while a pilot cutter lay at the mole, never during the fog-bound hours when the cutter was away from the mole, and the cutter's log shows that it never put out while the bell was tolling. Each toll was entered beside the names of ships that anchored within hearing, and the pilots' guild charged every one of them a fee whether or not it later used the channel. Repairs to the mole, by contrast, were paid from tonnage dues collected at the customs quay. These details suggest that the bell's tolling served chiefly

Which choice most logically completes the text?
answer_a: to warn captains away from the Gannet Shoals, since its sound helped ships in thick fog locate the safe channel.
answer_b: to call pilots out to endangered vessels, since the bell sounded only when a pilot cutter lay at the mole.
answer_c: to secure fees for the pilots' guild, since ships anchored within its hearing could be billed even if never guided.
answer_d: to finance repairs to the mole, since each ship that anchored added to the income the harbor could collect.
explanation: Choice C is the best answer because the three details together point to a revenue purpose rather than a safety one. Merholt, with the same shoals and fog, managed without a bell and suffered no more groundings, so safety does not account for the practice. The bell was tolled only when a pilot cutter was at the mole, which suggests it was timed to the guild's availability rather than to the weather. Ships that anchored within hearing were logged by name and charged by the guild whether or not they used the channel, which shows that anchoring within the bell's hearing, not receiving help, produced the payment.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. This restates the received navigation-aid account. But Merholt faced the same shoals and fog without a bell and ran aground no more often, and the bell fell silent whenever the cutter was away from the mole, even in dense fog, which a warning meant for ships in danger would not do.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. It fits the most noticeable detail, the link between the bell and the pilot cutter, but the cutter's log shows that it never put out while the bell was tolling, so the bell did not send pilots to anyone. The passage also says anchored ships were charged whether or not they used the channel, which points to billing rather than rescue.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. Repairs to the mole were paid from tonnage dues collected at the customs quay, and the fee charged to anchored ships went to the pilots' guild, so nothing in the passage ties the bell to financing repairs.

question_text:
Historians of the Karsmere Railway have long explained the minute-by-minute logbooks kept in its telegraph offices as an aid to safe train dispatching, supposing that exact times let officials reconstruct the sequence of movements after an accident. Yet the minute entries appear only for messages from private, fee-paying senders; train orders, though far more urgent, were logged to the nearest hour. The neighboring Dessane line, with comparable traffic and a similar accident record, kept no minute entries at all and ran just as punctually. And each Karsmere office paid a clerk a monthly supplement to prepare a fair copy of the log, which went not to the dispatching department but to the accounts department. Fees, by contrast, were reconciled from numbered receipt stubs, and station clocks were reset each noon from a time signal. These details suggest that the minute entries served chiefly

Which choice most logically completes the text?
answer_a: to help investigators sequence train movements after accidents, since exact minutes would have mattered most in an inquiry.
answer_b: to let managers audit clerks' handling of customer fees, since the fair copy was sent to the accounts department.
answer_c: to keep the offices' clocks aligned with one another, since the minutes could be compared across the line's stations.
answer_d: to document how the company had served paying senders, since the finest record covered only revenue-bearing traffic.
explanation: Choice D is the best answer because the details, taken together, point to a commercial rather than operational purpose. The minute entries cover only fee-paying private senders' messages while far more urgent train orders were logged to the hour, the equally punctual Dessane line managed without minute entries, and the costly fair copy went to the accounts department rather than to dispatchers. Because fees were already checked from receipt stubs and clocks were already set by a time signal, the entries were not needed for either job. Together these details suggest the entries gave the company a precise record of its service to paying customers.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. This restates the historians' safety account and adds the assumption that inquiries needed exact minutes, but train orders were logged only to the nearest hour and the Dessane line was equally punctual and safe without minute entries.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. The copy going to the accounts department is the most noticeable detail, but the passage states that fees were reconciled from numbered receipt stubs, so minute times were not needed to check clerks' handling of fees. The passage also says only that the copy was sent to accounts, not that it was reviewed there for fees.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. The passage states that station clocks were reset each noon from a time signal, so the minute entries were not needed to keep clocks aligned, and nothing indicates the entries were compared across stations.

question_text:
Historians of Hallowmere have long maintained that the numbered iron lamp posts the city erected from 1744 onward were intended to deter crime after dark. Yet the posts stand only on lanes inside the chartered limits; the equally narrow and crowded lanes of Dunnock Ford, just across the Teal Brook and outside the charter, never received a single one. During the lean years after 1790, the council had the interior alleys left unlit to economize but continued paying the lamplighter to tend every post along the outermost road, which runs along the charter boundary, though carters' accounts and the watch's own reports record almost no one on it at night. And the posts are numbered outward from the charter stone rather than by position along any street. The night watch, by contrast, assigned its patrols by parish. These details suggest that the lamps chiefly served

Which choice most logically completes the text?
answer_a: to deter intruders on the outer road, since they were thought to enter the city chiefly along it.
answer_b: to draw night trade into chartered lanes, since the lanes across the brook were equally crowded.
answer_c: to display the reach of the council's authority, since the posts marked where its charter applied.
answer_d: to guide travelers along the main routes, since those routes were the ones used most after dark.
explanation: Choice C is the best answer because the three details together point to the lamps as a marker of jurisdiction. The posts appear only inside the charter, never in equally crowded Dunnock Ford; the council kept the outermost road, which runs along the charter boundary, lit even while darkening interior alleys, although almost no one used that road at night; and the posts are numbered outward from the charter stone. Each fact fits lamps that showed where the council's authority extended, whatever the lighting need.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. This tries to rescue the received account of crime deterrence by assuming that intruders entered along the outer road, but the passage offers no such evidence. The council also left the crowded interior alleys dark during the lean years while keeping the outer road lit, which undermines the idea that the lamps targeted crime.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. This fits the most striking detail, that crowded Dunnock Ford went unlit, but it is defeated by the outermost road, which the council kept lit despite almost no night traffic there, and by the outward numbering from the charter stone. Neither detail would matter for drawing trade into particular lanes.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. Guiding travelers is a plausible rival purpose, but the passage rules it out: the council kept lit the outermost road, where almost no one traveled at night, and the equally crowded lanes of Dunnock Ford never received a post. The posts are also numbered outward from the charter stone rather than along any street, which would not help a traveler follow a route.

question_text:
Scholars of the Tarsen valley have long held that the notches carved along the rims of its millstones were dressing guides, marking where a miller should recut the stone's grooves. Yet the grooves lie on the stone's face, while the notches sit on its rim, where no cutting tool is ever applied. Each time a stone was dressed, moreover, the mill's carver recut every notch to the same full depth, however worn the stone, though groove depth was gauged with a wooden template and the recutting added a day of labor. And the mills of the neighboring Dovrel valley, which grind the same grain on identical stone that wears at the same rate, bear no notches at all. In Tarsen, grain from the seven villages was ground in a fixed sequence, whereas Dovrel millers took whatever arrived first, and each Tarsen stone bears exactly seven notches. Every stone remained at the mill for which it was quarried. These details suggest that the notches chiefly served

Which choice most logically completes the text?
answer_a: to guide the miller in recutting the grooves, since a dressed stone had to be renewed at regular intervals.
answer_b: to give the villages' fixed grinding order a visible form, since Tarsen ground grain in set turns and Dovrel did not.
answer_c: to show when a stone was due for replacement, since repeated recutting would reveal how much rim was left.
answer_d: to tell one mill's stones from another's, since stones from different mills would otherwise look much alike.
explanation: Choice B is the best answer because it accounts for all three details together. The notches are on the rim rather than the grooved face, and a template, not the notches, gauged groove depth, so they were not working guides. Yet carvers paid a day of labor to recut them after every dressing, which shows the marks mattered. At Dovrel, which grinds the same grain on identical stone that wears at the same rate but takes grain in order of arrival, there are no notches, while Tarsen, which ground grain from the seven villages in a fixed sequence, maintained them, and each Tarsen stone bears exactly seven notches, matching the number of villages. The most logical conclusion is that the notches gave the preset order of villages a lasting, visible form.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. This restates the received account with an added assumption about dressing intervals. The passage states that the notches sit on the rim where no cutting tool is applied and that groove depth was gauged with a wooden template, so the notches were not needed to guide recutting.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. The costly recutting after every dressing might seem to suggest a wear gauge, but each notch was recut to the same full depth however worn the stone was, so the notches could not record accumulated wear. The Dovrel stone also wears at the same rate yet has no notches.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. The passage states that every stone remained at the mill for which it was quarried, so there was little need to tell stones from different mills apart. Identification also does not explain why the notches are absent at Dovrel or why they were recut at such cost. Moreover, every Tarsen stone bears exactly seven notches, so the marks could not distinguish one stone from another.

question_text:
Historians of the Veskerran highland post have long explained the elaborate handstamp that each town office struck on outgoing letters, a ringed mark bearing the town's full name within a twelve-petal border, as a safeguard against forged dispatches. Yet the lowland Karrow post, which carried the same sealed correspondence under the same threat of forgery, marked its letters with a plain stamp bearing only the town's full name in unadorned, fully legible letters. Highland inspectors, meanwhile, authenticated dispatches by checking the sender's countersigned docket. Transit logs, which tracked each letter between offices, record only its dates of arrival and dispatch, never the mark. And town councils, not the post itself, had commissioned the original designs and paid to have a die recut whenever its petals began to blur, even while the name remained entirely readable. These details suggest that the stamp's elaboration served chiefly

Which choice most logically completes the text?
answer_a: to help inspectors tell genuine dispatches from counterfeits, since each office's distinctive border would be hard to copy elsewhere.
answer_b: to let carriers recognize a letter's town of origin at a glance, since a name set within a prominent mark is easily read.
answer_c: to let the post follow a letter between offices en route, since each town's mark could be matched to a stage of its journey.
answer_d: to express each town's civic pride, since an ornate mark would serve as an emblem of the town that commissioned it.
explanation: Choice D is the best answer because it is the only inference that all four details support together. The lowland Karrow post faced the same forgery threat yet used a plain stamp, and highland inspectors relied on dockets, so elaboration was not needed for security. The transit logs that tracked letters between offices never record the mark, so it played no part in the post's own handling of mail. And town councils, not the post, commissioned the designs and paid to recut dies while the name was still readable, which indicates that the towns, not the post, valued the ornament and bore the cost of keeping it sharp. Taken together, the details indicate that the ornate mark served chiefly as an emblem of each town's civic pride.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. It rescues the received account by assuming that inspectors relied on the border pattern, but the passage says they authenticated dispatches through the sender's countersigned docket, and the Karrow post faced the same threat of forgery yet used a plain stamp.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. It fits the most salient detail, that the mark displays the town's full name, but the plain Karrow stamp also bore the full name in fully legible letters, so the border added nothing to recognizing a letter's origin. Councils also paid to recut dies even while the name was entirely readable.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. The transit logs, which tracked each letter between offices, were the post's own record of a letter's journey, and they record only dates of arrival and dispatch, never the mark. The mark therefore played no part in following a letter's progress.
